summary: INTERSECT returns distinct rows present in both SELECT results.
syntax: SELECT column FROM first_source INTERSECT SELECT column FROM second_source
documentation: INTERSECT returns distinct rows present in both SELECT results. Compatible branches must produce the same number of columns. A final ORDER BY controls display of the common rows.
caution: Repeated source rows appear once. Compound-query duplicate comparison treats NULLs as equal; tests here use non-NULL text.
scenarios: Find products offered by two selected suppliers.
Identify staff IDs present on two required training lists.
Compare shared customer identifiers across two local exports.
title: Find shared supplier products
problem: Tables supplier_a(sku TEXT) and supplier_b(sku TEXT) contain non-NULL ASCII SKU strings. Return one sku column with distinct values found in both tables, ordered by SQLite’s default binary text order. Keep case differences distinct.
goal: Use INTERSECT or an equivalent approach demonstrating the same premise.
hint: Intersect the two single-column selections and add a final ORDER BY.
starter:
-- Write one SELECT or WITH query against the supplied tables.
SELECT 1;

tests.name: Duplicates
tests.setup: CREATE TABLE supplier_a(sku TEXT); CREATE TABLE supplier_b(sku TEXT);INSERT INTO supplier_a VALUES('B'),('A'),('A'); INSERT INTO supplier_b VALUES('A'),('A'),('C');

tests.name: Case
tests.setup: CREATE TABLE supplier_a(sku TEXT); CREATE TABLE supplier_b(sku TEXT);INSERT INTO supplier_a VALUES('A'),('a'); INSERT INTO supplier_b VALUES('a');

tests.name: No intersection
